transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um... I guess, well, what finally pushed me to come in today—and honestly, I've been putting this off for months, maybe even years if I really sit down and think about it—is that I just... I can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. 

My life is just full of these complex moving parts right now. I'm a software developer by trade, but I have my hands in a lot of different projects, and it's just gotten to the point where the plates are spinning out of control. I have all these things going on... I've got these patent notes I need to review and finalize, prep work for this technical workshop I'm supposed to be running, gallery deadlines for some interactive digital pieces I do on the side, plus just the everyday, high-level team decisions at my actual job. 

And instead of looking at all of that and prioritizing it, I just... I don't know, my brain just doesn't categorize it properly. I end up just starting whatever is loudest, you know? Like, whatever Slack notification is flashing on my screen or whoever is asking for something right this very second, instead of what actually matters. I'll spend half the day drafting a response for a completely irrelevant team decision that could have easily waited a week, while the patent notes are just sitting there gathering dust and the gallery deadline is breathing down my neck. It’s just incredibly frustrating because I know what the priorities *should* be, but I just can't seem to orchestrate it all without getting derailed by the noise.
Looking back, did you experience similar difficulties with focus and organization during your childhood?

Yeah, actually, if I really trace it back... it is funny you ask that because I was just thinking about this the other day. It was absolutely there in grade school. Long before I was even a teenager, honestly. 

I vividly remember the whole ordeal with homework folders. My mom used to buy me these specific, heavy-duty plastic ones because I kept destroying or losing the regular paper ones, but it did not even matter because I would just lose the entire folder anyway. It would just vanish into the ether of my desk or somewhere on the school bus. And the most agonizing part, the thing that used to drive my parents absolutely up the wall, was that I would actually do the homework. I would sit there at the kitchen table, finish all the math problems or whatever it was, put it in my bag, and then the next day when the teacher asked for it, it just would not register that I needed to take it out and hand it in. I would literally have the finished assignment sitting right there in my backpack, getting completely crumpled up at the bottom, and I would get a zero just because I forgot to physically turn it in. 

Every single parent-teacher conference was the exact same script, too. They would always start by telling my parents that I was bright and had all this potential, but then they would immediately follow it up by saying I daydreamed all day and spent all my time staring out the window in my own little world. So yeah, looking back, this is not just a recent thing with my software projects. It is like the exact same issue has been there since I was a little kid, just with different stakes.
Do you often feel a persistent sense of physical restlessness or difficulty sitting still?

Physical restlessness... yeah, absolutely. It’s actually a huge problem for me, especially with how my job is structured these days. Because, you know, being a software developer—especially now that I'm dealing with more of the high-level architecture and team decisions—I am just constantly stuck on these incredibly long design calls. I'm talking like two, sometimes three-hour syncs where we're just staring at wireframes or backend diagrams on a screen share. 

And during those calls, I just... I get this intense, almost physical pressure building up inside my body. It’s hard to describe, it's like this coiled spring feeling, or like water building up behind a dam, and I just have this overwhelming urge to get up. I literally cannot just sit there in my ergonomic office chair. Which, by the way, I spent way too much money on, thinking a better chair would magically make me sit still and focus, but it doesn't make a bit of difference. 

So what happens is, I'll start feeling that pressure, and I just have to move. I end up pacing around my home office. Just back and forth, behind the desk, over to the window, pacing while I listen on my headset. Or, if I have to be on camera—which is a whole other layer of exhausting because you have to perform the act of 'listening' for everyone else—I’ll constantly be shifting around. I actually keep a drafting stool and a regular chair in my office just so I can swap between them. I'll be bouncing my leg, shifting my weight, moving from the chair to the stool, just doing whatever I can to bleed off that physical tension, all while I'm desperately trying to look totally focused and professional for the rest of the team on the Zoom grid. It’s exhausting, honestly. I spend half my energy just managing the physical act of staying in the frame before I even get to the mental part of actually processing what they're saying about the software.
